strengths: Well-motivated problem with practical relevance to model efficiency and understanding of LLM internals
Comprehensive taxonomy of 13 scoring functions providing systematic characterization of head inactivity across attention weights, value vectors, and outputs
Strong validation methodology using model interventions—actually zeroing identified heads and measuring MMLU accuracy impact, rather than relying on observational measures alone
Broad experimental coverage spanning 14 pretrained models across 3 model families (Llama, OLMo, Qwen) with controlled threshold analysis showing consistency of scoring function rankings
Clear presentation and excellent visualizations (especially Figure 1 taxonomy and Figure 3 rankings), with comprehensive implementation details supporting reproducibility
Model-agnostic finding that Avg Head Output Norm consistently outperforms other scoring functions across different model families
Analysis of score distributions providing insights into attention behavior and model scaling effects
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Evaluation restricted exclusively to MMLU (multiple-choice QA task); findings may not generalize to generation, reasoning, translation, or other critical tasks where different attention heads are engaged

Modest performance margins with ~12% of heads pruned while maintaining accuracy within 1% of baseline—this narrow margin provides weak evidence for true inactivity versus redundancy, and lacks cumulative analysis when multiple heads are zeroed
Threshold selection methodology is ad-hoc (quantile-based) with no principled guidance for practitioners on how to select thresholds for new models, severely limiting practical utility
Work is purely descriptive without downstream applications—no demonstration of actual compression, distillation, inference speedup, or memory savings; no deployment of compressed models

Insufficient mechanistic insight into why certain scoring functions outperform others (e.g., why Avg Head Output Norm beats Avg Weight of First Token despite prior work) and limited investigation of architectural factors explaining inter-model differences
Incomplete analysis of model-specificity and transfer properties—unclear whether heads inactive in one model can be safely pruned in related models or across model scales
Confounding factors not adequately addressed: Llama-3.2's distillation from Llama-3.1-8B may create artificial inactive heads; FinWeb-Edu dataset limited to educational domain
Missing ablation studies on normalization schemes (LN, HN, AHON) and no sensitivity analysis on normalization choice contributions to scoring function effectiveness
Limited comparison to existing pruning methods beyond weak random baselines; no quantitative comparison to prior head pruning or compression approaches
Statistical rigor gaps: no significance testing on differences between score functions, no confidence intervals on pruning estimates, and limited error analysis or discussion of result variability

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 14 models from 3 model families with consistent methodology
Systematic organization of 13 scoring functions with clear mathematical definitions and implementation details
Thoughtful layer-wise normalization approach for fair head comparison across layers
Practical relevance to model efficiency and interpretability
Good reproducibility with code implementations and hyperparameter details provided
Combines multiple evaluation perspectives (ranking, IoU, interventions, distributions)
weaknesses: Severely limited novelty: presents 13 straightforward heuristic metrics (sums, norms, entropy) as a 'taxonomy' without proposing new methods; prior work (Guo et al. 2024, Michel et al. 2019) already explored similar scoring functions
Weak positioning: fails to clearly distinguish from or compare against Guo et al.'s dormant attention work, which found similar ~12% removal rates—appears as derivative follow-up

Fundamental conceptual confusion: conflates inactivity, redundancy, and attention sink behavior without precise definition of what 'inactive' means; lacks principled justification for why these metrics indicate inactivity

Problematic evaluation: uses only MMLU (single task) to define ground truth inactivity; doesn't distinguish between heads that are truly inactive vs. redundant with peers; no statistical testing or confidence intervals

High disagreement between metrics undermines taxonomy validity: max IoU of 0.88 (Figure 2) shows metrics identify different head sets; paper doesn't adequately explain what 'inactivity' is if metrics disagree so much
Insufficient analysis of identified heads: shows they can be removed but doesn't interpret what these heads do, their attention patterns, task-specificity, or why they're redundant
Incomplete finetuning analysis: conclusion that 'finetuning causes little change' is stated but barely investigated despite being central to motivation
Arbitrary design choices without ablation: threshold selection via quantiles, the specific set of 13 functions, and 1% MMLU tolerance lack justification or sensitivity analysis
No practical methodology: proposes 13 metrics but provides no guidance on which to use when or how to combine them; unhelpful for practitioners
Missing computational analysis: despite efficiency motivation, provides no inference time or memory measurements from head removal
Dense, difficult presentation: Figures 2, 3, 5, 6 are hard to interpret; relationship between different evaluation perspectives unclear

strengths: Comprehensive taxonomy of 13 scoring functions capturing different aspects of attention head inactivity, going beyond prior work's simple attention weight thresholding
Rigorous experimental evaluation across 14 models in 3 families with model intervention studies to verify identified heads are truly inactive
Strong empirical findings including evidence that head output norms are more indicative than attention weights, and that finetuning has minimal effect on attention patterns
Excellent reproducibility with PyTorch implementations, detailed model specifications, and public dataset usage
Multiple complementary evaluation perspectives including ranking analysis, intervention curves, score distributions, and attention pattern visualization
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—core concepts (attention sinks, head importance scoring) are established; contribution is primarily systematic evaluation rather than new methods
Threshold selection appears ad-hoc with quantiles (5-30%) chosen without principled justification or sensitivity analysis
Shallow mechanistic understanding—paper identifies which heads are inactive but provides limited insight into why, with underdeveloped attention sink analysis
Crude intervention approach via head zeroing without comparison to softer pruning strategies; lack of degradation may reflect over-parameterization rather than true inactivity
Limited evaluation scope restricted primarily to MMLU without assessment on diverse downstream tasks, limiting claims about generalizability
Missing statistical rigor including no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated trials on performance differences, with some accuracy deltas appearing marginal
Weak practical guidance—unclear which score function practitioners should use for new models or how to set thresholds without ground truth
Incomplete analysis of comparative performance between score functions, overlap patterns, and complementarity

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 14 models and 3 model families with rigorous model intervention methodology to validate findings
Clear improvement over prior work: demonstrates that AWFT-based methods miss ~7% of inactive heads and AHON (LN) is more model-agnostic and stable across datasets
Excellent reproducibility with PyTorch implementations, detailed methodology, and extensive appendix; strong adherence to research standards
Insightful secondary findings about finetuning's minimal effect on attention and dataset-agnostic behavior of output norm metrics
Well-executed experimental design with appropriate baselines (random head removal) and multiple datasets (MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande)
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily compares simple existing metrics rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts; score functions are straightforward calculations
Severe practical limitations: computing AHON requires full head output, making it 'impossible to save compute when skipping a head' (acknowledged in A.14); no demonstrated inference speedup

Narrow evaluation scope: single forward pass analysis only (multi-turn context not evaluated); primarily multiple-choice tasks (generation is future work despite being more practical); context-dependent inactivity shown in Figure 13 but underexplored

Methodological concerns: threshold selection imposes fixed ~10-30% quota rather than identifying optimal point; layer normalization (LN) introduced ad-hoc without principled justification; lacks ablation studies on norm types and normalization strategies

Limited theoretical understanding: no mechanistic explanation for why heads become inactive; anomalies like Qwen2.5-14B mentioned but not rigorously investigated; OLMo-2 differences inadequately explained
Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; sensitivity analysis of threshold selection missing; no investigation of whether results vary across runs

Incomplete evaluation: no task-specific analysis of inactive heads; no out-of-distribution evaluation; no investigation of head interactions or behavior during finetuning beyond aggregate Wasserstein distances
Circuit-based vs. pre-projection definition ambiguity (A.1) with limited impact analysis; terminology inconsistencies between 'dormant' and 'inactive'

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 14 models and 3 families with proper validation through model interventions
Clear problem motivation showing that attention weight-based measures alone are insufficient for identifying inactive heads
Well-presented work with detailed experimental setup, code implementations, and reproducible results across multiple datasets
Interesting finding that AHON(LN) generalizes better as a score function than prior work's attention sink-based measures
Secondary insight that finetuning (SFT, DPO, RLHF) leaves attention patterns largely unchanged is noteworthy
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an empirical comparison of straightforward score functions (L2 norms, entropy), extending rather than fundamentally advancing prior work on inactive heads

Critical limitation inadequately addressed: Section A.5/Figures 13-15 reveal inactivity is highly context-dependent (sequence length). Heads called 'inactive' become active on longer sequences, undermining the premise of identifying context-free inactive heads

Unclear practical utility: no actual efficiency improvements demonstrated; authors acknowledge AHON(LN) requires computing full head output, making compute savings 'impossible to save compute when skipping a head'

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: paper lacks explanation for *why* AHON(LN) works better or principled framework for designing score functions; claims about larger models 'specializing' heads lack supporting analysis

Methodological concerns: uses dynamic pruning (heads vary per-forward pass) not reflecting realistic static pruning; evaluates only single forward passes due to MC benchmark format, missing generation scenarios where errors compound
Generalization limitations: only decoder-only LLMs tested; only academic benchmarks; context-dependence findings limit applicability to real deployment scenarios
Statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance testing, or repeated runs; some improvements in Table 2 are marginal (Llama-3.2-3B: -0.29%) without uncertainty quantification

Arbitrary design choices: layer normalization strategy appears ad-hoc (head normalization mentioned as worse only in appendix); threshold selection procedure varies across datasets but lacks principled guidance

strengths: Rigorous validation methodology: Uses model interventions to verify inactivity, not just analyze attention patterns. This is methodologically sound and stronger than prior work.
Comprehensive experimental scope: 14 models across 3 families, multiple datasets, careful threshold selection, and extensive ablations demonstrate thoroughness.
Clear evidence of distinct score functions: Figure 2 shows low agreement (max IoU 0.58, precision 0.73) between functions, justifying the need for multiple approaches.
Model-agnostic insights: AHON (LN) achieves top ranking on 8/14 models and top-3 on 13/14, suggesting more general principles than prior attention-weight methods that fail on OLMo.
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation with code snippets, hyperparameters, and dataset information enable reproduction and future work.
Challenges prior work effectively: Demonstrates that relying on first-token attention sinks misses ~7% of inactive heads, with clear empirical evidence.
Useful secondary findings: Observations that finetuning causes minimal attention changes and scaling has limited effects until large sizes are valuable insights.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Score functions are straightforward (norms, entropy). The contribution is systematic evaluation rather than new methods, making it incremental.

Context-dependent inactivity undermines generality: Figures 13-15 show inactivity is sequence-length-dependent. Heads classified inactive on short sequences become active on longer ones, questioning the generalizability and practical significance of findings.

Evaluation limited to single-pass, multiple-choice benchmarks: No evaluation on generative tasks (instruction-following, long-context generation) where most practical LLM applications occur. Acknowledged in A.14 as 'complex,' but this is a major scope limitation.

Unresolved efficiency concerns: The best score function (AHON) requires computing head outputs, making actual compute savings impossible (A.14). Practical impact depends on future work discovering efficient alternatives.

Insufficient explanation of why AHON works: Demonstrates stability (Figure 5) but lacks theoretical justification for why head output norms are more indicative than attention patterns across different distributions.
Incomplete task analysis: No investigation of whether different tasks have different inactive head patterns or which specific heads/layers are consistently inactive across tasks.
Unprincipled threshold selection: Quantile-based thresholds work for comparison but don't guide practitioners on threshold selection for new models/datasets without benchmarking.
